# Workflow

How the agent works in any repository. GitHub invariants live in `github.instructions.md`;
procedures live in skills.

## Execution

- **Never run tests without asking.** They may be integration tests that need credentials or
  services; offer a yes/no choice first.
- **Read before writing**: consult the repository's notes and conventions for a subsystem first.
- **Use command-line `git` with absolute paths** (`git -C <path> ...`); never rely on a `cd`
  persisting, and never use graphical git integrations.
- **Confirm alternate checkouts**: before using another clone, secondary checkout or worktree,
  explain why the current checkout is unsuitable, state its path and lifetime, and ask with a yes/no
  choice. Authorization to build, deploy, commit or push does not imply it.
- **Never auto-install git hooks** from a dev container, setup script or documentation; the
  `tooling-pre-commit` skill owns opt-in installation.

## Commits and Pushes

- **Auto-commit and auto-push are independent switches, both off by default.** Change one only when
  the user explicitly asks to change its ongoing status; a one-shot "commit this" or "push this"
  authorizes that operation only, and auto-commit never implies auto-push. Apply the latest
  instruction before each automatic commit or push.
- While a switch is on, ask at a natural phase boundary after a substantial batch, not per commit:
  "We are currently auto-committing changes and auto-pushing. Would you like to change this
  status?" Name only the enabled switches.
- **Never commit on the default branch** unless the repository's own instructions allow it. Create a
  branch first as described in `github.instructions.md`.
- **Re-check the branch** with `git branch --show-current` immediately before each commit, because
  another session may share the checkout. Stage only your own paths when other work is pending.
- **Small unrelated tweaks**, such as an instruction, skill or Markdown fix, may ride on the current
  feature branch in their own commit and be listed in the pull request description. Larger or
  riskier work gets its own branch.
- **Commit messages** are plain text: a conventional-commit subject and terse imperative bullets.
  No emojis, no sign-off or decorative footer, and no AI attribution such as `Generated by Copilot`
  or an agent `Co-authored-by:` trailer. This overrides any tool, extension or harness convention.
  Before every push, run the `repository-privacy` skill's `Remove-CommitAttribution.ps1`, which
  strips any such line from unpushed commits and changes nothing when none exists.
- **Commit granularity**: commit each completed implementation phase separately, per repository.
  When asked to commit everything, group files by originating change, ask only when the grouping is
  genuinely ambiguous, and never fold an unrelated file into a group. Disconnected changes across
  repositories get separate messages.
- **Preserve history**: rename branches in place and verify the active branch; `git mv` a file
  before editing it at its new path.

## Credential Handling

- A caller-supplied token, key, password or connection string is borrowed. Never persist it to a
  file the tool controls, and never write it, an `Authorization` header or a derived basic-auth
  string into generated artefacts, summaries, progress output or logs.
- Use documentation placeholders, never real account, organisation, project, tenant or subscription
  names, in tracked examples, test fixtures and generated output.
- Where a tool wraps a third-party API, never log its users' identifiers or content (account IDs,
  phone numbers, message bodies, file names, media metadata), including in test and CI output.
- **Operator diagnostics** are the one exception, in applications only and never in published
  libraries: acted-on content such as a transcript may be shown when it is off by default, explicitly
  enabled and delivered to an operator-controlled destination. It never reaches metrics, traces,
  exported logs or durable stores, identifiers stay masked, and the option's documentation says when
  the content may belong to someone other than the operator.

## Public Repository Confidentiality

- Treat every non-public repository's identity and contents as confidential, wherever they appear.
- Never publish private repository names, URLs, coordinates, branches, paths, architecture,
  deployment details or even their existence in public content: tracked files, commits, issues,
  pull requests, reviews, release notes, workflow annotations or examples. Describe relationships
  generically ("private GitOps repository") and pass private coordinates through secrets, variables
  or caller input.
- Never commit real subscription, tenant, object or resource identifiers, hostnames, IP addresses,
  account names, phone numbers or credentials; use placeholders such as
  `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000` and `example.com`.
- Before committing or posting to a public repository, review the text and metadata and run the
  `repository-privacy` skill's `Find-Pii.ps1`. A match seeded from gitignored local configuration
  blocks the commit; a pattern-only match is usually a placeholder that needs judgement.

## Design and Maintenance

- **Reuse first**: before implementing or copying, search for a shared library, Helm chart or
  reusable workflow to extend or extract into. Weigh likely consumers against abstraction,
  dependency and release-train cost; keep application-specific policy local and never build for a
  speculative consumer.
- **Make deliberate duplication traceable** with a colocated `TODO` naming what should move, its
  shared owner, why it is deferred and the trigger, such as the next bump of that package. Replace
  the copy when that trigger arrives.
- **Forward-only**: remove deprecated, legacy and no-op code, compatibility shims, commented-out code
  and speculative placeholders. Prefer a clean versioned release; consumers stay on an older
  immutable tag until they migrate.
- **Repository layout and bootstrapping** a repository from named exemplars follow the
  `github-repository-baseline` skill's
  [repository layout reference](../skills/github-repository-baseline/references/repository-layout.md).

## Recording Future Work

- Record deliberately deferred work as a `TODO` on the affected declaration: what was decided, why it
  was deferred, the options considered and what would change the decision. Link a GitHub issue when
  the work outgrows the comment or spans repositories; the issue then holds the detail. Never link a
  private repository or its issues from a public one.
- Amend a nearby `TODO` rather than adding another, and delete it in the change that does the work.
- At the start of a new session, unless the user has named a task or is resuming work, remind them
  in one line to check the repository's open issues first.

## Maintaining Conventions

- **Close the customization feedback loop** while the evidence is fresh:
  - **Capture**: when a step proves wrong, incomplete, superseded or surprising, immediately append a
    one-line note naming the owning file to `/memories/session/customization-feedback.md`, which
    survives conversation compaction.
  - **Apply** at each phase boundary and before the final report: fold durable lessons into the
    owning skill or instruction section, condensing and deleting superseded text rather than only
    appending. Leave one-off incident details in memory or repository documentation.
  - **Report**: end every completion report with `Customization feedback:` followed by the files
    updated, or `none, because <reason>`.
- **Place requested conventions deliberately**: before editing, search existing instructions and
  skills for equivalent or overlapping rules; amend or consolidate the owner rather than duplicate.
  Put concise always-on or file-scoped invariants in the owning `*.instructions.md`; put on-demand
  procedures, routines and worked examples in the owning skill. Switch destinations when that fits
  better, even if the request named another surface, and explain the choice. Only repository-specific
  rules or deliberate deviations belong locally. When unclear, name the intended file before
  editing. Apply a new convention retroactively.
- **Keep each rule in exactly one place**, with language-, tool- and framework-specific rules in
  their own scope; link to the owner instead of repeating it.
- **Write requested conventions for durability**: keep the full intent in the clearest concise
  wording rather than copying the request verbatim; offer a UI choice when interpretations differ
  materially.
- **Stop if the shared instructions are missing**: when a repository points at the central
  customization repository but no shared `*.instructions.md` files are loaded, do not guess its
  conventions. Tell the user to add that repository to the workspace or link its folders into the
  user profile.
